Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette: Ahmed is a 27-year-old Middle Eastern male who works as a physical therapist. He has been married for two years and has recently sought help due to severe symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a sexual assault that occurred six months ago. The incident happened one evening when Ahmed was working late at the clinic where he had just finished seeing patients. As he was about to leave, a former colleague, who had been fired for inappropriate behavior with other clients, approached him in an isolated area of the building. This colleague forced Ahmed into a small storage room and sexually assaulted him despite his attempts to resist. Since that night, Ahmed has experienced intense anxiety triggered by specific olfactory cues such as cologne or perfume. The scent can transport him back to the moment when he was trapped in that room with his attacker. Whenever this happens, he dissociates, pretending it occurred to someone else and distancing himself from the immediate experience. This mechanism provides a brief respite but leaves him feeling detached from reality. Ahmed's work as a physical therapist places him in close proximity to patients, often involving hands-on treatment. Physical pain, even minor discomfort or soreness, can suddenly remind him of that night. He becomes overwhelmed with fear and anxiety, unable to function normally at his job. This has led to frequent absences from work, which has strained his relationship with both colleagues and supervisors. Intimacy with his wife has become increasingly challenging. Ahmed finds himself reacting with alarm during sexual situations, viewing them as potential triggers rather than moments of closeness. He avoids these encounters, leading to frustration for both him and his spouse. This avoidance has created tension in their marriage, causing feelings of guilt and shame. Ahmed frequently engages in body monitoring, constantly checking himself for signs of danger or injury, which is a direct reflection of the trauma he experienced. Even small physical sensations can trigger his startle response, making him jumpy and easily alarmed by unexpected touches or movements nearby. This hypervigilance has made social interactions difficult, as he often feels on edge in public settings. Ahmed harbors deep negative appraisals about himself and his body. He is convinced that he will never feel normal emotions again, particularly those associated with trust and safety. His belief that he cannot rely on himself exacerbates his anxiety, making it challenging to engage fully in daily activities without anticipating danger or harm. The shame he feels about what happened to his body has led to a sense of self-loathing and isolation. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has significantly impacted Ahmed's life. His work performance has deteriorated, leading to increased stress from potential job loss. At home, the strain on his marriage has become unbearable. It was this realization that finally compelled him to seek help. While he is afraid of revisiting the trauma and confronting his fears, he hopes for a return to a sense of normalcy and emotional stability. Ahmed is eager to regain control over his life and repair the relationships that have been damaged by his PTSD symptoms. In summary, Ahmed's journey since the assault has been marked by intense avoidance behaviors, maladaptive coping strategies, and pervasive negative appraisals about himself and his body. His current state reflects a critical point where he recognizes the need for intervention to restore his mental health and quality of life.
